maximizeTab.title: Maximise a tab in one click
maximizeTab.body: Double-click any workbench tab to expand it fullscreen. Press Esc to restore the surrounding layout.

mcpControl.title: Drive restorm with AI
mcpControl.body: Restorm ships an MCP server, so AI assistants like Claude Code can list, open, edit, and run your requests, inspect responses, and manipulate the workspace programmatically — without leaving their chat.

envSwitch.title: Switch environments easily!
envSwitch.body: Change the environment on the current request or on every request in your API by clicking the status-bar button, or by right-clicking the request's send button!

authRequests.title: Need to authenticate to use your API?
authRequests.body: Instead of firing a request every time to fetch a token and copy/paste it everywhere, use auth requests! When a call fails (401, 403, …) or your token's lifetime is up, the auth request is automatically replayed to extract the token and reuse it. Handy!

supplyChain.title: Protect yourself!
supplyChain.body: Like any software, Restorm relies on third-party libraries. To prevent supply-chain attacks, every outbound call is caught at the lowest level, and we alert you if a third-party library tries to steal your personal information!

codeSnippets.title: Restorm helps you write code!
codeSnippets.body: Find code snippets on every request to help you integrate them into your software. Many languages available: curl, PowerShell, TypeScript, C#, and many more!

workbenchLayout.title: Organise your workbench
workbenchLayout.body: Got a big screen and lots of requests? Put them side by side, stacked, or pretty much however you want! Just drag a tab where you need it. All for your comfort!

persistState.title: Find it just as you left it!
persistState.body: If you close Restorm and reopen it, you'll find it in the exact same state as you left it.

favorites.title: Some are dearer to your heart…
favorites.body: Got requests that matter more to you than others? Pin them as favourites!

console.title: See what is going on
console.body: The console lets you watch calls to your APIs as you fire requests. Handy for copy-pasting them into your terminal when needed! Pick your flavour: curl or PowerShell?

miniBrowser.title: Tired of switching windows all the time?
miniBrowser.body: Restorm ships a built-in mini web browser. Handy when your app reacts visually to your API calls.

apiDocs.title: Documentation, right here
apiDocs.body: No need to switch between Restorm and your API's documentation. If your API ships a spec (Swagger, OpenAPI, …), it's imported into Restorm and you can read it directly here.

secrets.title: Protect your secrets
secrets.body: Your passwords and auth tokens aren't stored inside the Restorm file itself. Restorm keeps secrets and request history in separate files — make sure not to commit them to GitHub. Restorm can also pull secrets from AWS, GitHub, and other vaults.

themes.title: Your colours, your mood
themes.body: Restorm comes with several colour schemes. Pick the one that matches how you feel.

search.title: Find everything, fast
search.body: See the top of this window? Restorm ships a search engine — no more hunting for hours to find THE one request.

multiEnv.title: Same requests, different environments
multiEnv.body: Got a dev, a prod, and a staging environment? Same requests, just not quite the same URLs, not quite the same tokens… Use environments and variables to switch between them in one click. You can even mark each environment with its own colour and icon to dodge those Friday-evening-before-the-weekend production scares!

protocols.title: More than just REST
protocols.body: Restorm speaks REST… and a lot more! GraphQL, gRPC, SOAP, OData, WebSocket — many protocols at your fingertips, without switching tools.

responseTree.title: See your API responses, visually
responseTree.body: Did you know you can browse your API responses in a more visual way? Restorm renders them as an interactive tree you can navigate, fold, and unfold.

responseHistory.title: Request history
responseHistory.body: You can browse the history of every call to your APIs. Handy for figuring out what actually happened.

multiLanguage.title: 27 languages!
multiLanguage.body: Restorm speaks 27 languages. English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Japanese, Chinese, Korean, and many more — pick yours in the settings!

fromPostman.title: Coming from Postman or Bruno?
fromPostman.body: We help you make the switch to Restorm — your transition made easy ;)

chainRequests.title: Several requests to chain together?
chainRequests.body: Use your requests inside scenarios, add conditions, and even nest scenarios within other scenarios.

stepByStep.title: Step through your scenarios
stepByStep.body: One step at a time, to see exactly what happens. You can even set breakpoints.

cicd.title: Run your scenarios in your CI/CD pipelines
cicd.body: Start Restorm headless to run a scenario with no UI and collect its logs — automated tests, built visually.

nestedScenarios.title: See what's going on in a scenario
nestedScenarios.body: A scenario can call another. In the inspector, read every log and jump straight to the scenario it came from.

scenarioHistory.title: But what just happened?
scenarioHistory.body: Browse the execution history of your scenarios. One of them changed since? No worries — we kept its configuration.

codeSandbox.title: Scenarios and security
codeSandbox.body: You can write code in your scenarios — but it runs in a secure sandbox, with no access to your local files and no direct internet access. The safest way to stay protected!

codeLanguages.title: Fancy writing some code?
codeLanguages.body: Write code right inside your scenarios — in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Lua, Ruby, C# or R!

scenarioAi.title: AI-drivable scenarios
scenarioAi.body: Claude, Cursor, Copilot… know your codebase: ask them for tailor-made scenarios. Everything is exposed over MCP to create, edit and run scenarios.

interactiveScenarios.title: Interactive scenarios!
interactiveScenarios.body: Make your scenarios parameterisable and even ask the user what to do with dialog boxes.

customValueLists.title: Reusable value lists
customValueLists.body: Define your own value lists and reuse them in your requests and your scenarios alike.

100.name: Continue
100.description: The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body.

101.name: Switching Protocols
101.description: The requester has asked the server to switch protocols and the server has agreed to do so.

200.name: OK
200.description: Standard response for successful HTTP requests. The actual response depends on the request method used.

201.name: Created
201.description: The request has been fulfilled, resulting in the creation of a new resource.

202.name: Accepted
202.description: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed.

204.name: No Content
204.description: The server successfully processed the request and is not returning any content.

301.name: Moved Permanently
301.description: This and all future requests should be directed to the given URI.

302.name: Found
302.description: Tells the client to look at another URL. The HTTP/1.0 specification required the client to perform a temporary redirect.

304.name: Not Modified
304.description: Indicates that the resource has not been modified since the version specified by the request headers.

400.name: Bad Request
400.description: The server cannot or will not process the request due to an apparent client error (e.g., malformed request syntax).

401.name: Unauthorized
401.description: Authentication is required and has failed or has not yet been provided.

403.name: Forbidden
403.description: The request contained valid data and was understood by the server, but the server is refusing action.

404.name: Not Found
404.description: The requested resource could not be found but may be available in the future.

405.name: Method Not Allowed
405.description: A request method is not supported for the requested resource.

408.name: Request Timeout
408.description: The server timed out waiting for the request.

409.name: Conflict
409.description: Indicates that the request could not be processed because of conflict in the current state of the resource.

410.name: Gone
410.description: Indicates that the resource requested was previously in use but is no longer available and will not be available again.

415.name: Unsupported Media Type
415.description: The request entity has a media type which the server or resource does not support.

422.name: Unprocessable Entity
422.description: The request was well-formed but was unable to be followed due to semantic errors.

429.name: Too Many Requests
429.description: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time (rate limiting).

500.name: Internal Server Error
500.description: A generic error message, given when an unexpected condition was encountered and no more specific message is suitable.

501.name: Not Implemented
501.description: The server either does not recognize the request method, or it lacks the ability to fulfil the request.

502.name: Bad Gateway
502.description: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and received an invalid response from the upstream server.

503.name: Service Unavailable
503.description: The server cannot handle the request (because it is overloaded or down for maintenance).

504.name: Gateway Timeout
504.description: The server was acting as a gateway or proxy and did not receive a timely response from the upstream server.

swagger.description: The OpenAPI 2.0 spec, born at SmartBear. Paste a Swagger JSON or YAML — Restorm parses every operation, pulls in security schemes, and turns the whole document into a navigable tree of requests.
swagger.trademark: Swagger is a registered trademark of SmartBear Software.

openapi.description: The current OpenAPI standard (3.0 and 3.1). Same paste-and-go ergonomics as Swagger: parameters, request bodies, security schemes, and webhooks land as a tree of typed requests with examples ready to send.
openapi.trademark: OpenAPI is a project of the OpenAPI Initiative under the Linux Foundation.

curl.description: Already have the request running in your terminal? Paste the full curl invocation — flags, headers, body, query string — and Restorm rebuilds it as a real request you can rerun, edit, and pin.
curl.trademark: curl is open source software © Daniel Stenberg, used here under its terms.

powershell.description: Same idea, PowerShell flavor. Paste an Invoke-WebRequest or Invoke-RestMethod command and Restorm reads the URI, method, headers, and body to seed a request you can iterate on visually.
powershell.trademark: PowerShell is a registered trademark of Microsoft Corporation.

postman.description: Got a Postman collection saved at the office? Drop the JSON — Restorm reads every request, every example response, and every environment variable, then rebuilds the collection as a Restorm tree you can run side-by-side with the rest of your APIs.
postman.trademark: Postman is a registered trademark of Postman, Inc., used here for compatibility reference only.

insomnia.description: Coming from Insomnia? Drop your export. Restorm understands its v4 / v5 collection format, brings every request, header, body, and environment along, and surfaces the lot as a Restorm tree.
insomnia.trademark: Insomnia is a registered trademark of Kong Inc., used here for compatibility reference only.

bruno.description: Bruno-flavored .bru files or a folder export — Restorm reads the .bru text format, including its scripting blocks, and recreates each request as a first-class Restorm node ready to send.
bruno.trademark: Bruno is open source software (MIT) by Anoop M. D., used here under its terms.

graphql.description: Paste a GraphQL SDL (.graphql / .gql / a paste from your GraphQL client) and Restorm scaffolds one request per operation, wired to the right query / mutation / subscription type with variables already structured.
graphql.trademark: GraphQL is a trademark of the GraphQL Foundation, a project of the Joint Development Foundation.

grpc.description: Drop a .proto file (or a directory of them) and Restorm walks every service, every RPC, every message — turning each method into a typed request you can send through the gRPC executor without touching codegen.
grpc.trademark: gRPC is a project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

soap.description: Got a WSDL? Paste it (or its URL) — Restorm parses every <port> and <operation> and produces ready-to-send SOAP envelopes with the right SOAPAction header, schema-typed body skeletons, and the auth scheme the WSDL declares.

websocket.description: Paste a WebSocket endpoint (ws:// or wss://) — Restorm opens the connection, captures the server's hello frames, and scaffolds send / subscribe requests with replayable payload templates.
websocket.trademark: WebSocket is a protocol standardized by the IETF (RFC 6455) and the W3C.

kafka.description: Paste an Apache Kafka bootstrap-server URL (or a list of topics) — Restorm registers consumers + producers per topic, decodes Avro / Protobuf payloads via your Schema Registry, and lets you replay individual offsets in one click.
kafka.trademark: Apache Kafka and the Kafka logo are trademarks of the Apache Software Foundation.

socketio.description: Paste a Socket.IO server URL — Restorm negotiates the handshake, lists the namespaces and event names the server emits, and gives you one request per emit / on event with payload validation.
socketio.trademark: Socket.IO is an open-source library released under the MIT license; the name and logo are used nominatively.

odata.description: Paste an OData service-document URL or a $metadata file — Restorm reads the CSDL, rebuilds the entity sets, function imports, and actions, plus pre-fills the $filter / $select / $top / $skip query options on every operation.

mqtt.description: Paste an MQTT broker URL or a topic catalog — Restorm scaffolds publish / subscribe requests per topic, keeps the connection live for streaming previews, and remembers retained-message snapshots so you can replay them later.
mqtt.trademark: MQTT is an OASIS standard; the MQTT name and logo are trademarks of OASIS Open.

importCard.title: Import your API
importCard.body: Bring in an OpenAPI / Swagger spec, a GraphQL schema, a Postman / Bruno / Insomnia collection, or paste a curl / PowerShell command. Restorm parses it, builds the folder layout, and lands every endpoint pre-filled.

help.input: Injects the scenario's input parameters and constants into the graph.
help.output: Declares one of the scenario's named results, read by a parent Run-scenario.
help.if: Branches the flow to then / else by comparing two operands.
help.switch: Routes the input to a matching case, or to default.
help.httpRequest: Runs a saved API request and emits its response.
help.soapRequest: Runs a saved SOAP request and emits its parsed response. A SOAP fault is surfaced on the response; a failed call is routed to the `error` port.
help.runScenario: Runs another scenario as a reusable sub-step.
help.forEach: Runs the body once per item of a collection, then continues.
help.for: Loops over a number range, running the body for each value.
help.while: Repeats the body while a condition holds (tested first).
help.doWhile: Repeats the body while a condition holds (runs at least once).
help.aggregate: Reduces a collection to one value (count, sum, min, max, average, join).
help.map: Transforms every item of a collection into a new list.
help.filter: Keeps the items that match a condition; routes the rest aside.
help.removeFromList: Removes matching values from a list.
help.wait: Pauses for a duration, then continues.
help.waitUntil: Pauses until a given date/time, then continues.
help.now: Emits the current date and time.
help.timer: Fires its body on a repeating interval or a cron schedule.
help.comparator: Compares two values and emits true or false.
help.boolean: Combines booleans with and / or / xor / not.
help.object: Builds an object from its named inputs.
help.setVariable: Stores a value into a run variable.
help.transform: Renders a Handlebars template from the input and run variables.
help.code: Runs your code (TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Lua, Ruby or R) in a sandbox and returns the result.
help.cast: Converts a value to another type (number, string, boolean, date, list).
help.regex: Matches, extracts, replaces or splits text with a regular expression.
help.json: Parses a JSON string, or serialises a value to JSON.
help.xml: Parses an XML string, or serialises a value to XML.
help.yaml: Parses a YAML string, or serialises a value to YAML.
help.crypto: Hashes or encodes a string (base64, md5, sha…, hmac, uuid).
help.jwt: Decodes a JWT token into header, payload and signature.
help.datetime: Shifts, formats or diffs a date.
help.retry: Re-runs its body until it succeeds, with a backoff policy.
help.objectOp: Reshapes an object (get/set a path, merge, pick, omit, keys, values).
help.url: Encodes, decodes or parses URLs and query strings.
help.random: Generates a random number, string, boolean or pick.
help.listOp: Reshapes a list (sort, unique, reverse, flatten, chunk, slice, groupBy).
help.csv: Parses a CSV string, or serialises a list to CSV.
help.math: Runs a scalar math op (round, abs, sqrt, min, max, clamp…).
help.schema: Validates a value against a JSON Schema.
help.writeFile: Writes or appends text to a file.
help.throw: Deliberately fails with a message (for error branches and tests).
help.log: Writes a message to the run log and passes the value through.
help.assert: Checks a condition (chai-style) and routes to pass or fail.
help.socketioConnect: Opens a Socket.IO connection and re-emits each received event on its port.
help.socketioSend: Sends a message on an already-open Socket.IO connection.
help.websocketConnect: Opens a raw WebSocket connection and re-emits each received message on its port.
help.websocketSend: Sends a payload on an already-open WebSocket connection.
help.grpcConnect: Opens a streaming gRPC call and re-emits each received frame on its message port.
help.grpcSend: Writes a request message on an already-open streaming gRPC call.
help.grpcClose: Half-closes an already-open streaming gRPC call.
help.socketioConnectServer: Starts a Socket.IO server (port + route); ACKs every received event and re-emits it on its port. Send broadcasts to connected clients.
help.socketioSendServer: Broadcasts a message to every client connected to the referenced Socket.IO server.
help.socketioCloseServer: Stops the referenced Socket.IO server and disconnects its clients.
help.websocketConnectServer: Starts a raw WebSocket server (port + path); records each frame a client sends and re-emits it on its message port. Send broadcasts to connected clients.
help.websocketSendServer: Broadcasts a frame to every client connected to the referenced raw WebSocket server.
help.websocketCloseServer: Stops the referenced raw WebSocket server and disconnects its clients.
help.mqttConnect: Opens a long-lived MQTT connection from a bound request and subscribes to its topic; re-emits each received message on its `message` port.
help.mqttSend: Publishes a payload on an already-open MQTT connection (to its topic).
help.mqttConnectServer: Starts a local MQTT broker (port + topic filter); subscribes to its topic filter and re-emits each received message on its `message` port. Send publishes to connected subscribers.
help.mqttSendServer: Publishes a message to every subscriber of the referenced MQTT broker.
help.mqttCloseServer: Stops the referenced MQTT broker and disconnects its clients.
help.toast: Emits a toast notification in the Restorm UI while the scenario runs.
help.httpListen: Hosts a local HTTP mock server and listens indefinitely. `connected` fires once it is listening; each served request re-emits its data on the `served` port. The server stays up until an HTTP close (or a Stop), then `done` fires. No response output — it serves, it does not call out.
help.httpClose: Stops an already-listening HTTP mock server (declared by an HTTP server node), freeing its port.
help.grpcListen: Hosts a local gRPC mock server and listens indefinitely. `connected` fires once it is listening; each served call re-emits its data on the `served` port. The server stays up until a gRPC server close (or a Stop), then `done` fires. No response output — it serves, it does not call out.
help.grpcServerClose: Stops an already-listening gRPC mock server (declared by a gRPC server node), freeing its port.
help.soapListen: Hosts a local SOAP mock server and listens indefinitely. Each inbound request is dispatched to a configured operation (by its SOAPAction or body operation name) and answered with the canned SOAP envelope (a fault operation returns `<soap:Fault>`). `connected` fires once it is listening; each served request re-emits its data on the `served` port. The server stays up until a SOAP close (or a Stop), then `done` fires.
help.soapClose: Stops an already-listening SOAP mock server (declared by a SOAP server node), freeing its port.
help.graphqlListen: Hosts a local GraphQL mock server and listens indefinitely. `connected` fires once it is listening; each served operation re-emits its data on the `served` port. The server stays up until a GraphQL close (or a Stop), then `done` fires. No response output — it serves, it does not call out.
help.graphqlClose: Stops an already-listening GraphQL mock server (declared by a GraphQL server node), freeing its port.
help.odataListen: Hosts a local OData v4 mock service and listens indefinitely. `connected` fires once it is listening; each served request re-emits its data on the `served` port. The server stays up until an OData close (or a Stop), then `done` fires. No response output — it serves, it does not call out.
help.odataClose: Stops an already-listening OData mock service (declared by an OData server node), freeing its port.
